notes:
I've put together notes for all 11 verses from about 25 commentators. There are three gaps:

- I found nothing from Methodist, Lutheran or Orthodox writers, and no NET Bible notes on this chapter.
- I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of "give your servant success" (v. 11).
- The disagreements I did find are among individual commentators. They don't line up as Baptist vs Reformed vs Pentecostal positions.

For each writer, I name a tradition only where your site list puts them in one (for example, Guzik's Enduring Word is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list and The Gospel Coalition is on your Reformed list). I couldn't check every citation inside the long commentary pages, so some web addresses below cover several writers at once.

**v. 1**
- **What "the words of Nehemiah" means:** Ellicott reads it as the narrative or record of his affairs, written by him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-1.htm Benson and Poole take the Hebrew to mean "the acts," the things Nehemiah did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-1.htm
- **Who wrote it:** Coffman says the line is the book's title, like the openings of the prophets, and rejects the theory that a later scribe added it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/nehemiah-1.html The Gospel Coalition (Meek) lists three views: Ezra wrote it, Nehemiah wrote it, or the author of Chronicles gave it its final form. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nehemiah/
- **The date:** Ellicott says Chislev is roughly our December and the year is the 20th of Artaxerxes Longimanus. Susa was the Persians' main and favourite royal residence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-1.htm Grace to You (Baptist) dates the chapter to late 446 BC. https://shop.gty.org/library/bible-introductions/MSB16
- **Catholic view on dating:** The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that most historians long dated Nehemiah's mission to 445 BC. Its own view places Ezra's return after Nehemiah, under Artaxerxes II. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/10737c.htm
- **An older minority view:** The 1901 Jewish Encyclopedia mentions De Saulcy's identification of the king as Artaxerxes II. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tje/n/nehemiah.html An older encyclopedia on netbible.org disagrees and says the king was certainly Artaxerxes I. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Nehemiah&lang=de
- **God's timing:** Precept Austin says God placed Nehemiah beside the king who could authorise the work before Nehemiah even knew about the problem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-1-commentary

**v. 2**
- **His concern for Jerusalem:** Guzik says Nehemiah's body was in Persia but his heart was in Jerusalem, about 800 miles away, and links this to Psalm 137. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-1/
- **His family:** MacLaren suggests that a brother making the trip shows the whole family shared this concern. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-1.htm
- **His comfortable life:** Matthew Henry says Nehemiah lived in ease and honour but, like Moses, could not forget his suffering brothers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/1-1.html

**v. 3: Old ruins or a fresh disaster? (a real disagreement)**
- **The ruins were old:** Coffman says the walls had never been rebuilt since Nebuchadnezzar destroyed them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/nehemiah-1.html Keil & Delitzsch say the text says nothing about a recent demolition, and there is no need to invent new disasters. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/nehemiah-1.html MacLaren thinks a rebuilding attempt was halted by royal order (Ezra 4) and the ruins were the same ones Zerubbabel saw. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-1.htm
- **The damage was recent:** The Light of Israel commentary says this was probably recent destruction by hostile neighbours, with the king's approval (Ezra 4:7–24). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/1-1.html
- **Why an unwalled city mattered:** Guzik explains that it was defenceless, so people lived in constant fear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-1/ Precept Austin adds that the broken walls reflected the people's humiliation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-1-commentary

**v. 4**
- **How long he prayed:** Guzik notes about four months of prayer between this point and 2:1. The rebuilding later took only 52 days. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-1/
- **What kind of fast:** Lange thinks a fast lasting several days was probably not total. Nehemiah gave up pleasurable food rather than all food. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/nehemiah-1.html
- **"God of heaven":** Ironside says the title shows God's throne had moved from earth to heaven. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/nehemiah-1.html MacLaren calls it a Persian title for God that Nehemiah claims for Israel's LORD. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-1.htm
- **Grief that leads to action:** MacLaren says no one does worthy work on the walls without first weeping over the ruins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-1.htm

**v. 5**
- **Starting with who God is:** Precept Austin says the prayer opens with worship and rests on God's covenant faithfulness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-1-commentary
- **Justice, not only pity:** Keil & Delitzsch say Nehemiah appeals to God's righteousness and faithfulness more than to his compassion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/nehemiah-1.html

**v. 6: Confessing sins he didn't personally commit (a difference of emphasis)**
- **Identifying with the people:** The Gospel Coalition says Nehemiah had not personally sinned, but he identifies himself with the exiled people. It presents this as a model of group repentance for Christians today. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nehemiah/ Guzik also stresses that he says "we," not "they." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-1/
- **Real personal guilt:** Keil & Delitzsch read the added phrase "I and my father's house" as showing he deeply felt his own sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/nehemiah-1.html
- **"Day and night":** Keil & Delitzsch say the Hebrew word usually rendered "now" means "at this time," not "today." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/nehemiah-1.html

**v. 7**
- **No excuses:** Guzik warns against confessions like "if I sinned." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-1/
- **Sin is the root problem:** Precept Austin says the real problem was sin, not a lack of organisation or resources. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-1-commentary
- **Confession before rebuilding:** MacLaren says it is useless to ask God to repair what is ruined while keeping the sins that ruined it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-1.htm

**vv. 8–9**
- **Where the quotation comes from:** Keil & Delitzsch say it is a free summary, mainly of Deuteronomy 30:1–5, not a word-for-word quote. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/nehemiah-1.html Bible Hub links verse 8 to Leviticus 26:33 and verse 9 to Deuteronomy 30:2–4. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/nehemiah/1.htm
- **Praying God's promises back to him:** Guzik calls pleading God's promises the secret of powerful prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-1/
- **What the condition "if you return" means (different readings):** Lange says obedience here is the way to continued blessing, not the way of salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/nehemiah-1.html Guzik suggests that Nehemiah himself kept the condition, and because he identified with the nation, the nation could share in his obedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-1/

**v. 10**
- **God's reputation:** Precept Austin says Nehemiah appeals to God's reputation and past rescue, not to Israel's merit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-1-commentary Constable links "redeemed" to the rescue from Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-1.html
- **God's hand:** Grace to You traces a "good hand of God" theme through the book, starting here. https://shop.gty.org/library/bible-introductions/MSB16

**v. 11**
- **"This man":** Several writers see significance in calling the great king just "this man": Lange, Ironside and Constable. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/nehemiah-1.html https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/nehemiah-1.html https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-1.html The Pulpit Commentary simply says the king filled Nehemiah's thoughts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/1-11.htm
- **Whose mercy:** Matthew Henry says he asks for God's mercy as he speaks to the king, not the king's own mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/1-11.html
- **"This day" (different readings):** Gill takes it literally: he was to serve the king that day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/1-11.html The Pulpit Commentary says it may just mean "at this time." https://biblehub.com/nehemiah/1-11.htm
- **A prayer of action:** Guzik says Nehemiah asks God to use him, not someone else. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-1/
- **How important was the cupbearer? (different views):** Constable says outside sources make the post second only to the king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-1.html The Pulpit Commentary says Nehemiah was one of many cupbearers. https://biblehub.com/nehemiah/1-11.htm
- **Was he a eunuch? (a debate):** The Gospel Coalition says he likely was. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nehemiah/ Constable notes the idea rests on one Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) manuscript reading "eunuch" instead of "cupbearer." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-1.html
- **Why the king might say yes:** The Gospel Coalition suggests that unrest near Egypt gave Artaxerxes a reason to want a friendly people nearby. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/nehemiah/
